This tutorial

  • This tutorial will revise/introduce some relevant R commands for this subject.
  • Introduce data on Retail sales for Australia that will be used for the first forecasting application in this subject.
    • Retail sales are considered a key indicator of the health of an economy, and are commonly a target of interest for commercial forecasters.

Before starting with the questions, let’s warm up by setting up our workspace in RStudio. Usually the first step is to set up the working directory.

Warming Up: Setting Up Working Directory in R

Setting up the working directory ensures that R can accurately locate where your data files are stored. It defines where R looks for files and where it saves outputs.

To set up your working directory, enter command:

setwd("Your location goes here")

Alternatively, you can click on: \[\boxed{\;\textsf{Session}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Set Working Directory}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Choose Directory}\;}\]

On my computer, it looks like:

Warming Up: Checking Working Directory in R

To check your working directory, enter getwd() into your Console tab:

getwd()
[1] "/Users/chenpengyun/Desktop/ECOM30004_Tutoring_2026/TSAF_Week1"

Your working directory is also displayed here (above the Console window):

If the folder looks correct, you can proceed to loading the datasets and files.

Question 2

We will focus on the time series of Total retail sales. Create a time series object for monthly total retail sales. Plot this time series.

Retail_m <- ts(dt$Total, frequency=12, start=c(1982,4), end=c(2024,9))
plot(Retail_m, main="Monthly Australian Retail Sales",
  ylab="Retail sales ($m)")

aggregate generates a new series, Retail_q, by summing up the monthly observations of each quarter.

Question 3(b)

Create a window of this quarterly time series from 2000q1 to 2018q4, and produce a time series plot.

S_t <- window(Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2018,4))
plot(S_t, main="Quarterly Australian Retail Sales",
  ylab="Retail sales ($m)")

Question 4

Take the log of the quarterly time series and produce a plot.

Y_t <- log(S_t)
plot(Y_t, main="Retail sales (log), 2000q1 to 2018q4")

Questions 5 and 6

Denote the log retail sales time series as \(Y_{t}\). Create the first difference time series \[\Delta Y_{t}=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}\] Print out the first six values of \(Y_{t}\) and \(\Delta Y_{t}\). What’s going on with the value of \(\Delta Y_{t}\) for 2000q1?

# First difference of quarterly log retail sales Y_t, convert to pct
D_Y_t <- diff(Y_t)*100
print(round(head(cbind(Y_t,D_Y_t)),4))
            Y_t    D_Y_t
2000 Q1 10.3685       NA
2000 Q2 10.4144   4.5997
2000 Q3 10.4116  -0.2842
2000 Q4 10.5805  16.8887
2001 Q1 10.4393 -14.1158
2001 Q2 10.4745   3.5186

The first value in D_Y_t is missing (NA) because there is no value of Y_t available before 10.3685 to compute the difference. Taking a difference of a time series will necessarily result in a shorter time series because of this.

Question 7

Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by \(S_{t}\). Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is \[R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.\] Compare the values of \(\Delta Y_{t}\) and \(R_{t}\).

# Percentage change of retail sales
R_t <- diff(S_t)/lag(S_t,-1)*100
# Compare
print(round(head(cbind(D_Y_t, R_t)),4))
           D_Y_t      R_t
2000 Q2   4.5997   4.7071
2000 Q3  -0.2842  -0.2838
2000 Q4  16.8887  18.3986
2001 Q1 -14.1158 -13.1648
2001 Q2   3.5186   3.5813
2001 Q3   2.2103   2.2349

Question 7

Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by \(S_{t}\). Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is \[R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.\] Compare the values of \(\Delta Y_{t}\) and \(R_{t}\).

What does lag(S_t, -1) function do?

print(head(cbind(lag(S_t,-1),S_t)))
        lag(S_t, -1)     S_t
2000 Q1           NA 31839.1
2000 Q2      31839.1 33337.8
2000 Q3      33337.8 33243.2
2000 Q4      33243.2 39359.5
2001 Q1      39359.5 34177.9
2001 Q2      34177.9 35401.9

Question 7 ctd: Why the comparison?

  • Adding 1 on both sides and take logs: \[\begin{align} R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\\ 1+R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}}{S_{t-1}}\\ \log(1+R_{t})&=\log(S_{t})-\log(S_{t-1})\\ \log(1+R_{t})&=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}\equiv\Delta Y_{t} \end{align}\]
  • Then with the approximation \(\log(1+R_{t})\approx R_{t}\) for small values of \(R_{t}\), we have \(R_{t}\approx \Delta Y_{t}\): \[\text{$R_{t}\approx\log(1+R_{t})$}= \Delta Y_{t}\]

Question 7 continued

Why is \(\ln(1+x)\approx x\) for small values of \(x\)?

Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (1/2)

Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by \(S_{t}\). Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, \(R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%\).

Compare the values of \(\Delta Y_{t}\) and \(R_{t}\).

The values of \(\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}\) and \(R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}\) are quite similar especially for the smaller changes.

For the entire time series the two variables are very highly correlated:

print(cor(R_t, D_Y_t))
[1] 0.9985674
print(round(cor(R_t, D_Y_t), 3))
[1] 0.999

Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (2/2)

The values of \(\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}\) and \(R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}\) are quite similar especially for the smaller changes.

This is also evident in the plot shown below:

plot(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(D_Y_t), pch=16, cex=0.7,
     xlab="Rt", ylab="DYt")
lines(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(R_t), col="blue")

Question 7 ctd: Why taking logs differences?

  • Taking log differences or simple returns is a common type of “filtering” in time series analysis.
  • Filtering tends to stablise/linearise features such as trend and seasonality.
  • Changes in a logged time series can be interpreted as approximately percentage changes, which is often convenient.
  • Also, time series models, such as AR models and VAR models, requires data to be stationary \(\to\) filtering/transformation ensures this requirement is met.
